Your review is read-only on this checkout. Do not mutate the working tree, the index, HEAD, or branch state in any way. Use tools like `git show`, `git diff`, and `git log` to inspect history. If you need a working copy of a different revision, check it out into a separate temporary directory (e.g. `git worktree add /tmp/review-[SHA] [SHA]`) — never move HEAD on this checkout.

Plan alignment (implementation matches plan/spec; deviations justified; all planned functionality present). Code quality (separation of concerns, error handling, DRY, edge cases). Architecture (sound design, integration). Testing (real behavior, edge cases, integration). Production readiness (documentation, no obvious bugs). Do not re-run the soak tests.

1. Can I cite the exact file and line? If not, drop it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type parameter to select which agent type to use. If omitted, the general-purpose agent is used.

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh.
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

prompt.description: The task for the agent to perform

subagent_type.description: The type of specialized agent to use for this task

model.description: Optional model override for this agent. Takes precedence over the agent definition's model frontmatter and the configured default subagent model. If omitted, uses the agent definition's model, else the default (inherits from the parent unless a default subagent model is configured). Ignored for subagent_type: "fork" — forks always inherit the parent model.

effort.description: Reasoning effort for this agent. Set this ONLY when the user, or instructions such as CLAUDE.md or a skill, explicitly ask that this agent or delegated work run at a specific effort level, never on your own judgment; otherwise omit it and the agent runs at its usual effort.

Set to false only when your very next action depends on this agent's result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise leave it in the background so the user can hand you other work.

Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

- Investigating complex questions that require exploring many files

- For analysis: Start broad and narrow down. Use multiple search strategies if the first doesn't yield results.

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type parameter to select which agent type to use. If omitted, the general-purpose agent is used.

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh.
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- `cd` carries to the next call only in the main session, if the command succeeds and ends inside the working directories. Outside them the shell returns to the start folder; otherwise it stays where it was. Prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. - Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.

- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

+"""Command line: python3 -m ratelimit simulate --limit N --window S --calls C."""
+
+import argparse
+import sys
+
+from ratelimit import DEFAULT_WINDOW_SECONDS
+from ratelimit.clock import FakeClock
+from ratelimit.window import SlidingWindowLimiter
+
+STEP_SECONDS = 0.1
+
+

+    clock = FakeClock()
+    limiter = SlidingWindowLimiter(limit=limit, window_seconds=window, clock=clock)

+            allowed += 1
+        clock.advance(STEP_SECONDS)
+    return f"allowed={allowed} denied={calls - allowed}"
+

+    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(prog="python3 -m ratelimit")

+"""Token bucket: refills continuously, spends one token per allowed call."""
+
+from ratelimit.clock import MonotonicClock
+
+
+class TokenBucket:
+    def __init__(self, rate_per_second: float, capacity: int, clock=None):
+        self._rate = rate_per_second
+        self._capacity = capacity
+        self._clock = clock if clock is not None else MonotonicClock()
+        self._tokens = float(capacity)
+        self._last = self._clock.now()
+
+    def _refill(self) -> None:
+        now = self._clock.now()
+        self._tokens = min(self._capacity, self._tokens + (now - self._last) * self._rate)
+        self._last = now
+
+    def allow(self) -> bool:
+        self._refill()
+        if self._tokens >= 1.0:
+            self._tokens -= 1.0
+            return True
+        return False
+
+    def tokens(self) -> float:
+        self._refill()
+        return self._tokens

+"""Sliding window: at most `limit` allowed calls in any trailing window."""
+
+from collections import deque
+
+from ratelimit.clock import MonotonicClock
+
+
+class SlidingWindowLimiter:
+    def __init__(self, limit: int, window_seconds: float, clock=None):
+        self._limit = limit
+        self._window = window_seconds
+        self._clock = clock if clock is not None else MonotonicClock()
+        self._stamps = deque()
+
+    def allow(self) -> bool:
+        now = self._clock.now()
+        cutoff = now - self._window
+        while self._stamps and self._stamps[0] <= cutoff:
+            self._stamps.popleft()
+        if len(self._stamps) < self._limit:
+            self._stamps.append(now)
+            return True
+        return False

+"""Integration: Registry with sliding-window limiters across many keys, on a fake clock."""
+
+import unittest
+
+from ratelimit.clock import FakeClock
+from ratelimit.registry import Registry
+from ratelimit.window import SlidingWindowLimiter
+
+KEYS = [f"tenant-{n}" for n in range(50)]
+LIMIT = 3
+WINDOW = 1.5
+STEP = 0.25
+STEPS = 120
+
+
+class RegistryWindowIntegrationTest(unittest.TestCase):
+    def test_each_key_holds_its_limit_independently(self):
+        clock = FakeClock()
+        registry = Registry(lambda: SlidingWindowLimiter(limit=LIMIT, window_seconds=WINDOW, clock=clock))
+        allowed = {key: [] for key in KEYS}
+        for _ in range(STEPS):
+            for key in KEYS:
+                if registry.allow(key):
+                    allowed[key].append(clock.now())
+            clock.advance(STEP)
+        self.assertEqual(registry.keys(), KEYS)
+        expected = allowed[KEYS[0]]
+        self.assertEqual(len(expected), STEPS * STEP / WINDOW * LIMIT)
+        for key, stamps in allowed.items():
+            self.assertEqual(stamps, expected, key)
+            first = 0
+            for i, stamp in enumerate(stamps):
+                while stamps[first] <= stamp - WINDOW:
+                    first += 1
+                self.assertLessEqual(i - first + 1, LIMIT, key)
+
+
+if __name__ == "__main__":
+    unittest.main()

+"""Token bucket: refills continuously, spends one token per allowed call."""

+class TokenBucket:

+"""Sliding window: at most `limit` allowed calls in any trailing window."""
+
+from collections import deque
+
+from ratelimit.clock import MonotonicClock
+

+        self._limit = limit
+        self._window = window_seconds
+        self._clock = clock if clock is not None else MonotonicClock()
+        self._stamps = deque()
+
+    def allow(self) -> bool:
+        now = self._clock.now()
+        cutoff = now - self._window
+        while self._stamps and self._stamps[0] <= cutoff:
+            self._stamps.popleft()

+            return True

**Goal:** Build `ratelimit`, a standard-library-only Python package with a token bucket, a sliding-window limiter, a per-key registry, and a `simulate` CLI.

**Architecture:** Every limiter takes an optional clock object with a `now() -> float` method. `clock=None` means `MonotonicClock()`, and unit tests pass a `FakeClock` so no unit test sleeps. The sliding window keeps a deque of allowed timestamps and drops stamps at or before `now - window_seconds`. `Registry` maps each key to a limiter built by a zero-argument factory.

**Tech Stack:** Python 3.9+, standard library only (`time`, `collections`, `argparse`, `unittest`).

## Plan decisions the design leaves open

- `TokenBucket` starts full (`capacity` tokens) and refills continuously at `rate_per_second`, capped at `capacity`. The design does not say whether it starts full or empty; starting full is the usual behaviour.
- `SlidingWindowLimiter` treats the window as `(now - window_seconds, now]`: a stamp exactly `window_seconds` old no longer counts. Denied calls are not recorded.
- `Registry.keys()` returns keys in first-use order.
- The `simulate` loop starts its `FakeClock` at `0.0` and, for each call, calls `allow()` first and then advances the clock by 0.1 s.

"""Token bucket: refills continuously, spends one token per allowed call."""

from ratelimit.clock import MonotonicClock


class TokenBucket:
    def __init__(self, rate_per_second: float, capacity: int, clock=None):
        self._rate = rate_per_second
        self._capacity = capacity
        self._clock = clock if clock is not None else MonotonicClock()
        self._tokens = float(capacity)
        self._last = self._clock.now()

    def _refill(self) -> None:
        now = self._clock.now()
        self._tokens = min(self._capacity, self._tokens + (now - self._last) * self._rate)
        self._last = now

    def allow(self) -> bool:
        self._refill()
        if self._tokens >= 1.0:
            self._tokens -= 1.0
            return True
        return False

    def tokens(self) -> float:
        self._refill()
        return self._tokens
```

"""Sliding window: at most `limit` allowed calls in any trailing window."""

from collections import deque

from ratelimit.clock import MonotonicClock


class SlidingWindowLimiter:
    def __init__(self, limit: int, window_seconds: float, clock=None):
        self._limit = limit
        self._window = window_seconds
        self._clock = clock if clock is not None else MonotonicClock()
        self._stamps = deque()

    def allow(self) -> bool:
        now = self._clock.now()
        cutoff = now - self._window
        while self._stamps and self._stamps[0] <= cutoff:
            self._stamps.popleft()
        if len(self._stamps) < self._limit:
            self._stamps.append(now)
            return True
        return False
```

"""Registry: one limiter per key, created on first use."""


class Registry:
    def __init__(self, factory):
        self._factory = factory
        self._limiters = {}

    def get(self, key):
        limiter = self._limiters.get(key)
        if limiter is None:
            limiter = self._factory()
            self._limiters[key] = limiter
        return limiter

    def allow(self, key) -> bool:
        return self.get(key).allow()

    def keys(self) -> list[str]:
        return list(self._limiters)

"""Command line: python3 -m ratelimit simulate --limit N --window S --calls C."""

import argparse
import sys

from ratelimit import DEFAULT_WINDOW_SECONDS
from ratelimit.clock import FakeClock
from ratelimit.window import SlidingWindowLimiter

STEP_SECONDS = 0.1


def simulate(limit: int, window: float, calls: int) -> str:
    clock = FakeClock()
    limiter = SlidingWindowLimiter(limit=limit, window_seconds=window, clock=clock)
    allowed = 0
    for _ in range(calls):
        if limiter.allow():
            allowed += 1
        clock.advance(STEP_SECONDS)
    return f"allowed={allowed} denied={calls - allowed}"


def main(argv=None) -> int:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(prog="python3 -m ratelimit")
    commands = parser.add_subparsers(dest="command", required=True)
    sim = commands.add_parser("simulate", help="drive a sliding window with a fake clock")
    sim.add_argument("--limit", type=int, required=True)
    sim.add_argument("--window", type=float, default=DEFAULT_WINDOW_SECONDS, help="window in seconds (optional)")
    sim.add_argument("--calls", type=int, required=True)
    args = parser.parse_args(argv)
    print(simulate(args.limit, args.window, args.calls))
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

+"""Token bucket: refills continuously, spends one token per allowed call."""
+
+from ratelimit.clock import MonotonicClock
+
+
+class TokenBucket:
+    def __init__(self, rate_per_second: float, capacity: int, clock=None):
+        self._rate = rate_per_second
+        self._capacity = capacity
+        self._clock = clock if clock is not None else MonotonicClock()
+        self._tokens = float(capacity)
+        self._last = self._clock.now()
+
+    def _refill(self) -> None:
+        now = self._clock.now()
+        self._tokens = min(self._capacity, self._tokens + (now - self._last) * self._rate)
+        self._last = now
+
+    def allow(self) -> bool:
+        self._refill()
+        if self._tokens >= 1.0:
+            self._tokens -= 1.0
+            return True
+        return False
+
+    def tokens(self) -> float:
+        self._refill()
+        return self._tokens

+"""Sliding window: at most `limit` allowed calls in any trailing window."""
+
+from collections import deque
+
+from ratelimit.clock import MonotonicClock
+
+
+class SlidingWindowLimiter:
+    def __init__(self, limit: int, window_seconds: float, clock=None):
+        self._limit = limit
+        self._window = window_seconds
+        self._clock = clock if clock is not None else MonotonicClock()
+        self._stamps = deque()
+
+    def allow(self) -> bool:
+        now = self._clock.now()
+        cutoff = now - self._window
+        while self._stamps and self._stamps[0] <= cutoff:
+            self._stamps.popleft()
+        if len(self._stamps) < self._limit:
+            self._stamps.append(now)
+            return True
+        return False

import unittest

from ratelimit.window import SlidingWindowLimiter

LIMIT = 3
WINDOW = 1.5
SLACK = 0.01

### Strengths
- The code matches the plan's code blocks line for line (spot-checked `bucket.py:16`, `window.py:18`, `registry.py:11`, `registry.py:20`). It uses the names from design.md, adds nothing beyond the plan, and has no dependencies outside the standard library.
- Everything stays within Python 3.9. The `list[str]` annotation in `registry.py:19` is valid at definition time on 3.9, and `add_subparsers(required=True)` has been supported since 3.7.
- Every limiter treats `clock=None` as `MonotonicClock()`, and the injectable clock is applied consistently.
- `SlidingWindowLimiter` gives the window as `(now - window, now]` and does not record denied calls. This is what the soak tests' half-open check needs, and `test_unit_window.py` pins the exact boundary and the not-recorded behaviour.
- The test numbers avoid float trouble. The integration test uses 0.25 s steps and a 1.5 s window, both exact in binary. The CLI cases keep every eviction comparison at least 0.05 s from the boundary. The bucket tests use exact products (0.25 × 2.0).
- The CLI output is exactly `allowed=<a> denied=<d>`. `test_runs_as_module` exercises the real `python3 -m` entry point.
- `test_soak_short.py` and `test_soak_long.py` are unchanged across 1199cab..553a966. I re-ran the unit suite with `PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1`: 27 tests, OK. The working tree is unchanged.

### Issues

#### Critical (Must Fix)
None.

#### Important (Should Fix)
None.

#### Minor (Nice to Have)
1. **`ratelimit/bucket.py:16`: `tokens()` can return an `int` even though it is annotated `-> float`.** `min(self._capacity, ...)` returns `self._capacity`, which is an int, whenever the bucket is at capacity. Because `min` keeps the first of two equal values, this happens even with zero elapsed time. I confirmed it: `TokenBucket(1.0, 3, clock=FakeClock()).tokens()` returns `3`, not `3.0`. The tests pass only because `3 == 3.0`. A caller doing `isinstance(..., float)` or formatting the output would see the difference. Fix: `min(float(self._capacity), ...)`, or store `self._capacity = float(capacity)`. The plan wrote this line as it is, so this is a small plan defect, not an implementer mistake.
2. **Commit messages for 90e7571, e53012d, d81a1ab and 242ad4a have a malformed trailer.** In each, the `Co-Authored-By:` line sits directly under the subject with no blank line, so git and GitHub read it as body text, not a trailer. On top of that, all six commits name "Claude Haiku 4.5" rather than the session's attribution line. This is cosmetic. It only needs fixing if the team cares about trailers, and the fix is a reword when squashing or rebasing at merge.
3. **Spec wording vs. plan, no action needed.** design.md §6 describes the integration test as running "under the real clock". The plan moved that test onto `FakeClock` and left the real-clock coverage to `tests/test_soak_long.py`, which passed. Taken together, the spec is covered.

### Deferred-minor triage
None of the deferred minors has to be fixed before merge.
- **FakeClock negative advance; TokenBucket and SlidingWindowLimiter don't validate inputs; CLI doesn't validate `--limit`/`--calls`:** the plan says explicitly that "The design specifies no validation, so the plan adds none." Leaving validation out is a design choice. It could be a follow-up; the cheapest useful piece is argparse rejecting `--calls < 0`.
- **TokenBucket doesn't guard against a custom clock moving backwards:** the shipped clocks are monotonic, so this can't happen unless a caller misuses the API. Defer.
- **No `.gitignore` for `__pycache__/`:** a hygiene item. Add one in a follow-up or at merge, because the untracked directories are easy to commit by accident.
- **Commit trailer model name:** see Minor 2. Fix it when squashing if attribution matters.
- **`Registry.get` re-calls a factory that returns None; no test for a factory that raises:** only reachable with a broken factory. Defer.
- **`test_window_defaults_when_omitted` is weak; the integration test gives every key an identical sequence:** both come from the plan. The first is weak because it compares the default against the same value passed explicitly, so it can't catch a wrong default constant. The `DEFAULT_WINDOW_SECONDS = 1.0` decision is settled, so this is acceptable. Defer.

### Recommendations
- Optionally fix the int/float return in `bucket.py:16`. It's a one-token change.
- Add a `.gitignore` containing `__pycache__/`.
- If you squash at merge, use one correctly formatted attribution trailer.
- In a later iteration, consider basic argument validation in the CLI.

### Assessment
**Ready to merge?** Yes

**Reasoning:** The implementation matches the plan and spec, the settled human decisions are followed, and every test passes, including both controller-verified soak runs. What's left is minor (one type inconsistency and commit-message cosmetics), and no deferred minor blocks merge.
